uncited: Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes define the computational framework for sampling volumetric data along camera rays and aggregating those samples into final pixel colors.
This family solves the problem of mapping discrete 3D scalar or vector fields to 2D screen-space images by numerically integrating the volume rendering equation.

It is distinguished from object-order methods (like ray tracing of implicit surfaces) by its pixel-parallel, image-order nature, and from Monte Carlo methods by its deterministic, grid-aligned traversal logic.
All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function $V(\mathbf{p})$ must be approximated from a discrete set of samples $V_i$ located at grid positions $\mathbf{p}_i$.
**Query Positioning**: Determining the 3D coordinate $\mathbf{p}$ along the ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ where a value is needed.
This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings.
**Kernel/Weight Application**: Computing weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$ based on the distance between $\mathbf{p}$ and the sample centers $\mathbf{p}_i$.
The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring).
**Coordinate Transformation**: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized $[-1, 1]$ or $[0, 1]$ ranges) before interpolation.

Originating from the foundational work on direct volume rendering in the late 1980s and early 1990s, ray traversal methods evolved from simple fixed-step marching to adaptive and stochastic techniques.
The introduction of GPU fragment shaders enabled real-time image-order rendering loops .
